results.title: (PDF) Ethnographic fieldwork: an anthropological reader
results.content:
Title: (PDF) Ethnographic fieldwork: an anthropological reader
The collection highlights key themes such as reflexivity, identity, ethics, and the socio-political impact of ethnography, ultimately serving as a vital resource for teaching and understanding the nuances of fieldwork experiences. The notes which we kept during our ‘fieldwork’, as a method to track and reflect on these issues in our research experiences, were key sources for the article. The field of work and the work of the field: Conceptualising an anthropological research engagement \* Anthropology's sensitivity to the ethical dimension of our actions in the field and our authority in writing ethnographic representations Marcus and Fisher 1986; is rooted, among other things, in our perceptions of an imbalance in power between informants and ourselves . While the importance of ethnographic research in developing new knowledge is widely recognised, there remains minimal detailed description and discussion of the actual practice and processes involved in completing ethnographic fieldwork. The first author's experiences and struggles as an ethnographer of a group of young men from two locations (a gymnasium in Melbourne, and a remote Australian fishing town) are presented and discussed as a means of informing research practice. The fieldwork process was full of negotiation and compromise between fieldwork dynamics and the restraints and realities of researching within a university. My research and teaching interests centre on the cultural politics of food and drink and the production of food knowledges, with a specific focus on: food and migration; food histories, stories and heritage; environmental relations, social justice, and food labour; and eating, materiality, and the body. At once a methodological necessity and a disciplinary ‘rite of passage’, the fieldwork experience shapes both the researcher and project in equal measure. Review Symposium: Fieldwork is Not What It Used to Be, Qualitative Research, Feb 2012. This article reviews the history of the field offolklore with regard to the method of obtaining data or texts and demonstrates that collecting material contrasts with the practice of conducting research in the field. Pointing to a moment of transition, it shows that theories offolklore had to undergo significant change before methods of research would acknowledge the identity of the fieldworker and its significance.

results.title: Research Themes: Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences | Bangor University
results.content: Researchers in the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences undertake award-winning, internationally excellent, and impactful research. Our research ranges from language and literature, music and media, to financial studies, communication, technology studies, regulation, justice, identities, and community studies. Our research is firmly grounded in a sense of place through culture, materiality, mediality, literature, language, music, history, technology and institutions, along with an interest in the changing nature of communities, nations, structures of governance, and justice. Researchers develop completely new resources for studying Wales, and broaden travel writing to encompass more than English-language portrayals of Wales. Bangor has a proud tradition of world-leading research in Celtic studies, with particular focus and international links on the history, culture, literature, language, and politics of Wales. We house some of Wales’ leading research centres, which are directed by prominent Welsh historians, experts in Welsh law, Welsh culture, music, literature and poetry. The competing interests of local communities, nation states, and global and international economic systems require responsive research on regulations and governance, institutions, and community studies. Facilitated by its location in a bilingual environment, Bangor University has outstanding strengths in areas of multi- and bilingualism and language use across communicative contexts, encompassing research excellence in language policy and planning, first and second language acquisition, discourse analysis and corpus studies, community and civil society use of language and its implications for identity, as well as the role of technology in language development. Bangor is home to the state-of-the art Pontio Arts and Innovation centre helping to translate our research on arts and culture into creative activities which is then brought directly to our local communities. Researchers in the Bangor Business School play an active role in the regulation and governance of financial and economic institutions nationally and internationally, providing insights on important and topical themes through advanced modelling of credit and uncertainty; and financial regulation, competition, and corporate governance in banking. The Bangor Law School makes a substantive contribution to the development of legislative and policy processes of Wales and its developing institutions of justice through research on fundamental questions of justice and policies in place to protect the vulnerable.

results.title: Principles of Ethnographic Fieldwork | Intro to Cultural Anthropology Class Notes
results.content: ## 🗿Intro to Cultural Anthropology Unit 4 Review. ## 🗿Intro to Cultural Anthropology Unit 4 Review. 4.4 Ethics in Ethnographic Research. Ethnographic fieldwork is the backbone of cultural anthropology. Researchers use various techniques like participant observation and interviews to collect data while navigating ethical considerations. Ethnographers must balance insider (emic) and outsider (etic) perspectives to gain a comprehensive understanding of a culture. Building trust with community members is crucial, as is maintaining professional boundaries throughout the research process. ## Ethnographic Research Methods. * Ethnography involves systematic study of people and cultures through direct observation and participation. * Fieldwork requires researchers to immerse themselves in the community they are studying for extended periods. * Cultural immersion allows anthropologists to gain deep understanding of daily life, customs, and beliefs. * Thick description provides detailed, nuanced accounts of observed behaviors and their cultural context. * Participant observation involves actively engaging in community activities while taking detailed notes. * Audio and video recordings capture linguistic data, rituals, and other cultural performances. ### Ethical Considerations in Ethnographic Research. * Informed consent ensures participants understand the research purpose and potential risks. * Reciprocity involves giving back to the community through services or shared research findings. * Cultural sensitivity requires respecting local customs, beliefs, and social norms. * Reflexivity encourages researchers to examine their own biases and cultural assumptions. * Emic perspective focuses on understanding culture from the viewpoint of its members. * Etic perspective applies external, scientific frameworks to analyze cultural phenomena. * Combining emic and etic approaches provides a more comprehensive understanding of culture. * Reflexivity involves critically examining one's own cultural background and biases. * Researchers must consider how their presence affects the community being studied. * Acknowledging power dynamics between researcher and participants enhances ethical practice. * Ongoing self-reflection throughout the research process improves data interpretation and analysis. * Involves active listening, showing respect, and demonstrating genuine interest in local culture. * Facilitates access to sensitive information and private cultural spaces. ### Navigating Cultural Differences. * Participating in cultural rituals and celebrations demonstrates commitment to learning. * Balancing friendship with informants and maintaining objectivity as a researcher. * Considering long-term impacts of research on the community and individual participants.

results.title: The ethnographic fact: a discussion of ethics in anthropological fieldwork – Somatosphere
results.content:
Title: The ethnographic fact: a discussion of ethics in anthropological fieldwork – Somatosphere
# The ethnographic fact: a discussion of ethics in anthropological fieldwork. * 1 Comment on The ethnographic fact: a discussion of ethics in anthropological fieldwork. Indeed, when considering how past research has trespassed through other communities’ values, there are many good reasons for ethics – even the fluid ethics that anthropologists tend to work among – to be infrastructured (a verb) collectively with the help of a range of internal and external experts, rather than decided upon by individuals. Yet how to work ethically often cannot be known in advance, at least not when we want the people we meet to shape our work, when our methods are intentionally emergent, when the human-as-subject is not a fact to be assumed but one to study (Mol 2008). He raised two ethical issues that emerged while working with archives of Internet images: questions of copyright, and questions of how to use images that show people, especially when they engage in political activities and are identifiable. Rebeca Ibáñez Martín raised ethical complexities about the positionality of anthropologists in applied and collaborative research projects. Ibáñez Martín also pointed out that the ethics review process does not typically consider the mental health of PhD students as part of its evaluation and raises important questions about how to care for PhDs in the field. The ethics statement that Emily submitted to the Amsterdam Institute of Social Science Research (AISSR) ethics review committee offered writing as a method of addressing the emergent quality of ethnographic ethics:. The collective challenges surfaced at the workshop highlighted the need to make care-work central to field-work— to weave ethics into ethnographic practice. The ethnographic fact: a discussion of ethics in anthropological fieldwork.
